From the New York Erujuirer, January 25. MEXICO. New Orleans. The French consul in this city, has had the kindness to communicate to us, the two following documents, which we publish with pleasure not only that they evince the great intentions of Admiral Maudin, but because they contain intelligence which may be considered ol some importance to commerce. h. 1V1. frigate iVeieuie, Antomc Liz ahdo. 4 22d Lee 11138 \ To the French Consul, Sir þÿ It was my intention to give every possible facility to the commerce of all nations at Vera Crux. With regret I lind myself compelled to suspend these facilities. The enclosed copy of my circular of this day, addressed to the different foreign consuls resident in that city, will explain to you my motives. You will oblige me by giving the above publicity. Receive the assurance of my esteem and consideration. The Admiral Commander of the naval forces of Fiance in the Gulf of Mexico. (Signed) Charles JJaudin.

H. M. 1 rigate the IXereide, Antonc Lizardo, ) December 20, ISjy ( To the Consul, Sir þÿ You are aware of the treaty concluded by me on the 28th of Nov. last, w ith the Mexican General Don Alanuei Eincon, commander-in-chief of the department ot Vera Cruz. By the second article of said treatv, it was my desire to open the port ol Vera Cruz during eight months, to the (lags of all nations. In suspending ihe blockade during that lime, without awaiting an explanation of the difficulties existing between Mexico and France, 1 experienced a sincere satisfaction in putting an end to a state ot affairs, iatal to the prosperity of the city of Vera Cruz, and the interests of those nations trading with Mexico. From this time, although the Mexican government has declared war upon France and had violated the capitulation ol Vera Cruz I was not the less disposed to leave the port open to neutral vessels offering to enter on the faith ot this capitulation, and it w as with this object that 1 wrote on the 16th instant to the commander of the United States sloop ol war Erie, who has given publicity to my letter. But the Mexican cabinet having bv a most singular neglect of customary courtesy, left without reply, the pacific communications emanating from me, and particularly that of w hich the object was to render Vera Cruz a neutral city until the termination of the war: and as this Cabinet appears moreover to take a pleasure in aggravating daily, bv every sort of insult towards tnv compatriots, the

events of the savage act by which it has, in contempt ol its former engagements, ordered the immediate expulsion of the French. I declare, that under present circumstances, 1 see no possibility of making w ith such a government, the necessary arrangement for the fulfilment of my views in favor ot the commerce of every nation. Consequently, 1 have given orders to admit, either in the port of Vera Cruz, or at Sacrificios, or at Anton Lizard, all neutral vessels desirous of entering, hut I must await other events before permitting them to discharge their cargoes You will have the kindness j to make known that any attempt at discharging ilic smallest portion of merchandize, after notice given, will ho considered as a violation of ihe blockade, and as such will he followed bv the immediate confiscation ol both ship and

cargo. No small craft, w ith the exception of French or foreign vessels of war, will lie permitted, from the setting to the rising ol the sun, either to navigate, or anchor upon any part of the coast comprised between the point of Tempaola and the bar of Alvarado, under the penalty of beiug seized. Respectfully : (Signed) Charles Baliht.

But the most important intelligence in relation to Alexican affairs, is the following, which we copy from The American of last evening : þÿ Tiie French Squadron in the þÿPacific.- We have received from Al. De la Forest, the Consul General of France, an attested copy of the following important letter, which we translate : Frigate Nereide, Anton Lizardo, 15th December 1838. Sir þÿ In reference to my despatch of this day, hereby announce, that 1 have trans- 1 mitted information to the Commandant of our naval forces in the Pacific Ocean, of the Declaration of War, by Alexico, against France, with orders to proceed instantly to the Western coast of Alexico, with all his disposable strength. I beg you to communicate, in my name, this information to all the consuls and agents of France, on the two continents of America, through whom it may he conveyed either to any commander of our squadron, or to the commander of any French vessels of war in the Pacific Ocean. 1 rely upon your activity in this respect. Accept Al. Le Consul General, the assurance of every high consideration. CHARLES BAUD1X. To the Consul General of France, New York. There is thus no doubt that Alexieo has

declared war against France. We arc astonished however, that the declaration has not been published in this country, and look for it with some solicitude. Admiral Maudin, it seems too, has ordered the naval forces of 1' ranee, in the Pacific, to proceed to the Western coast of Alexico, hut it does not appear whether the object is to protect French commerce, or to enforce a blockade of the Alexican ports there.

From the New York Enquirer, Feb. 13. From the Dublin Mail. DEATH OF LOUD NORBURY With sentiments of sorrow and regret we announce this afflicting intelligence. The melancholy event took place at a quarter to twelve on Thursday. Thus, has another victim been sacrificed to that hellish system of ruffian legislation adopted by the lower order þÿ that wild justice of revenge, as it is styled) connived at, if not encouraged by the government þÿ undisguiscdly recommended bv the priests and demagogues, and shamefully advocated by a certain portion of the press, supposed to reflect the opinions of the leaders of the party. No language can convey to you the scene of misery that the house presents þÿ the suddenness of the bereavement, and the unprovoked atrocity of the bloody deed þÿ nor of the awful feeling of wonder and of dread that has taken possession of all. No man ever lived who was more generous in his nature, or who possessed a more warm, kind, or benevolent heart, or no less likely to give offence to any human being, be his rank in life what it might, than Lord Norbury. From Mexico. þÿ Our New Orleans siips of the 18th ultimo bring advices from Vera Cruz to the 5th inclusive, a French biig having arrived, which sailed on that da'. I lie brig had on board as passengers 100 natives of France, late residents in Mexico. Things remained much as before. The Mexican armv was still lying near the citv, and French residents were arriving from the interior. for the purpose of embarking. By an arrival from Bermuda at Philadelphia, we have the names of the British nn nof war now at Vera Cruz, the krig-ofwar Chnrybdis having arrived from Jamaica whence the squadron sailed. It consists of the Cornwallis and Edinburgh, 74, Pique 3G, Vestal 28, Rover ; Race horse and Modest I,' 18, Snake and Ringdove 16. At Vera Cruz the squadron was to be joined by the Madagascar and Seringapatain, 46. Letters from Vera Cruz, received at New Orleans, states that the British squadron is to co-operate with the French, in obtaining redress for spoliations on British commerce. This is very different from the idea heretofore entertained, and we should think it doubtful. It is said that our own government was invited to join as a third party, hut that the overture was declined, very properly, of course, our disputes with Mexico having been submitted to arbitration. It is reported that a Spanish ship and brig from Havana had arrived at Vera Cruz, arid were ordered away, not by the French but by tiie Mexicans ; and that on their way to Sacrificios they got ashore and were lost.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, January 31. FURTHER ACCOUNTS of the LATE GALE. On the first page we have placed all the particulars of the effects of the late gale, which were received by us by the yearly mails of this morning þÿ Subsequently the Eastern mail arrived, and has furnished us with the following additional accounts: þÿ From the Boston Transcript of Yesterday. THE STORM AND FLOOD AT THE EAST. A gentleman who left Gardiner, Me. on Monday morning, arid arrived in this city last evening, informs us that the late flood has done extensive damage on the principal rivers in Maine. In the course of two or three hours the waters of the Kennebec rose eleven feet, and on the Androscoggin in proportion The booms, up and down the two rivers, were nearly all carried away, and the waters covered with lumber and wrecks of bridges. The great dam at Kennebec resisted the force of the descending ice well, and it was not thought it had sustained much, if any damage. The mills at Brunswick were swept away by the force of the flood and ice. The bells at Hallowed were ringing from two in the morning until daylight, to call out the people to protect property. The water was four feet high in the main street. From the Boston Atlas, of yesterday. CONCORD, N. H. January 28, 18:19. STORM AND FRESHET The wind and storm on Sunday afternoon and evening were wi ll us more violent than anv since the memorable gale ol September 1815; and the destruction upon our rivers greater than at any time since February 1824.

So far as we can learn every bridge over the Merrimack, Northward to Plymouth a distance of 40 miles, is in part or wholly carried away. From the Boston Journal. In Saco the wind was more violent than it had been for twenty years. Fences were destroyed þÿ houses were unroofed þÿ chimnies wore blown down, and the river rose to an unusual height. Vast quantities of timber and wood were floated off.

In order, however, to make this clear to the proprietors, it is necessary to notice that nearly one-half of the amount of profits stated in the former report, consisted ot the interest on tiie first deposits, which accrued previous to the commencement of operations iri the West Indies, whilst the'wholc ot that now set forth has resulted from the business of the bank in the colonics. The directors have much satisfaction in adding, that from the accounts in their possession down to this time, thev confidently anticipate that the transactions of the half- ear just ended, will exhibit a steady increase of profit, even upon the improved results of that which preceded if At the period of their last report, the directors acquainted the proprietors, that her Majesty's government had referred the subject ot

the currency of the West India colonics to a committee of the Privy Council, on coins, who, it was expected, from the evidence laid before them, ot the defective state of currency, would recommend some remedy for the evil. The directors have not had the advantage of seeing that evidence, nor of being made acquainted with the report of the committee on coins ; they are consequently unable to form an opinion whether the measure, actually adopted by the government, was the result of the one or the other ; but they cannot refrain from saving in justice to themselves, that it is not in accordance with their recommendations on the subject, to her Majesty's government. From the period of the establishment of the bank, now nearly three years ago, the directors have constantly kept tinder the notice of the government, the defective state of the

currency in the West Indies, and have invariably recommended, as the most correct remedy,' that the dollar should be declared the only legal tender i«»r debt. This, however, the government would not assent to : but, in the month ol August last, they communicated to clamation here affixing the sterling vuU< at the directors, their intention of issuing a pro- . which Ute doubloon and dollar should lie legal tenders in the West Indies, and of causing proclamations to be issued by the governors of die respective colonies, affixing the values in currenty, at which the doubloon, dollar, and British silver coins should be legal tender. The directors immediately represented to the government, that they were of opinion this plan would not be acceptable to the colonies, as it must, in its application to the coins circulating in the West Indies, lead to extreme confusion in internal transaction, and that it would have the effect of introducing the British silver coinage to an inconvenient amount, from the circumstance of its being bv this measure made legal tender, at its current value to any extent, and without that limit, which, from its over value, it was tho't proper to impose upon it in this þÿcountry that subjecting the colonies to the ultimate possibility ot being over supplied with British silver was exposing them to the chance ot a heavy hiss, as any superabundant quantity of this silver, wiih which they might become burthened, could only be rendered available in external payments, at a very large sacri-

fice. arising Irorn the groat difference between its intrinsic and current value. The directors however, must in justice admit, that so long as the present arrangement is suffered to remain in force, by which the þÿ commissaries m the West Indies are requiied to supply bills on the treasury, at a premium of l'per cent, in exchange for this silver whenever demanded, it'wdl operate as any outlet for any excess, that may accumulate beyond the wants ot the circulation at a -moderate expense þÿ but they cannot lorget that the treasury may at any moment put a stop to litis facility, and give rise to the inconvenience they apprehend. The government having decided upon carrying out their own measure, the directors had a right to expect such an alteration m the charter, as would give the hank the benefit of the proposed plan ; this has been done by the grant of a supplementary charter, relieving the bank from the obligation ot paying its notes in silver dollars only, and permitting it to redeem them in the coins declared legal tender by the now at rangement. The directors have therefore to announce to the proprietors, that a supplementary charter to this effect, received the seal on the 30th of October, and was sent out to the West Indies bv the packet of the 1st ot November last. Sufficient tune has not set elapsed to allow the directors to receive the advice of the arrival of this instrument, and as ii will reach the colonics only towards the close of the half year just ended, they cannot antici-

pate, that its operations will produce much effect on the amount of profit to be stated at the next half yearly meeting; but, they look forward eventually to the most beneficial results from this altered charter, and confidently hope that at the meeting to be held in January 1840. they shall be enabled to present to the proprietors, an account shewing a material increase of profit arising from an enlarged circulation, independent of that steady improvement in the general business of the institution, which experience justifies them in expecting. In conclusion the directors beg to inform the proprietors that they continue to be perfectly satisfied with the zeal, intellegence and ability displayed by the officers and clerks through th< establishment, both in the West- Indies and in London ; that the system ol business adopted works well, and that, generally, they consider the institution in a prosperous condition, both as regards the nature of its operations, their mode of conduct, and the beneficial results to ho anticipated by ihe colonies and the proprietors, from its general working. From the New Yurk Commercial Advertiser, February 8, 1839. FROM CHINA. Wo glean the following items from our Canton files, the receipt of which we mentioned yesterday. From the Register of August 14. It was reported last Wednesday, that the superior officers of the province intended to stop the English trade, in consequence ot the movement of Admiral Mailland's squadron to Cltumpe ; hut as the squadron soon returned to its former anchorage at Tongkoo, þÿ the admiral, we presume, having gained his object, which, it appears, is a secret too important for the public ear, the governor and his colleagues suffered the trade to continue without interruption ; the passage boats, however, have been lately more strictly watched and often intercepted. The question now occurs, what benefit to the English trade, what protection ol English subjects and English property, has accrued from the presence of a flag officer and his squadron in the Chinese waters? for the admiral himself, and the nation he represents, there has only been repeated and accumulated insult. Himself, his officers, and his foreign women,' ( Fan foo, a low and insulting epith t, more objectionable than the character E.) have been forbidden to come to Canton, all supplies and communication have been officially interdicted, and the most actively hostile measures have been taken to prevent Ids smuggling himself or any of bis suite into the port. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, February 9, 1839. FROM MEXICO. The Cosmopolila of January the 9th has the following article : Mr. Packenham, the British minister, and the commander of the British squadron, arrived at Manga de Clavo on the 4th, where they bad been announced the day before. Their visit lasted two hours, and their object was to explain to Santa Ana the reason why he ought to assist in forming the treaty of peace which England wished to conclude between France and Mexico. The general insisted on the rights of his country arid declared that she had merely accepted the war provoked by France, Ide said that humanity only would induce her to conclude a treaty with Admiral Baudin, although the latter took pleasure in spilling Mexican blood þÿ he clearly explained the difference between the present state of affairs, and that which prevailed at the time of the ultimatum. He said it was for Mexico now to demand indemnity from France, and the first slep should be the restoration of St. Juan de Ulioa, not in its present condition, but perfectly reinstated ; and concluded by saying that the antipathies excited by Mr. Deflaudis would cnduie forever, and that neither laws nor treaties could put an end to them. The same paper states that in giving an account of what took place to the government, Santa Ana recommended the arming of the whole nation, to keep the spirit of the people from becoming coo!, and declared that war was a less evil than a shameful peace.

From Buenos Ayres. By|the ship Brutus, from Monte Video, sailed December 4th, Buenos Ayres papers to the 26th of November inclusive arc received. Atfairs between the French and the Buenos Avreans remained pretty much in statu quo. The blockade had caused a great accumulation of vessels in the port of Monte Video, where there were about 150 sail of foreign ships, and 50 coasters, when the Brutuss ailed. The French squadron consisted of 13 sail ; one 61, two 28s, two 22s, oue 20, three 18s, one 16, one 10 and two of 4 guns. There seems no prospect of a termination to the difficulties between France and the Argentine Republic.

GREAT SALE OF MULBERRIES. The great auction sale of Morns Multieaulis Trees, on Saturday, was attended by such an immense concourse of purchasers, that the large room of Mr. William H. Franklin, the auctioneer, could not contain them. '1 he trees were remarkably fine, and had just arrived from Mobile. They appeared to be of two years growth, although it was stated they were hut one year old. The prices ranged from 84 each tree for the largest size down to 81-75 for the smallest trees, which was the least price that any were sold for. Public opinion seems to set decidedly in favor of trees of American growth, as they will yield about thrice as many young plants the ensuing season as the imported ones, besides which those that have arrived from abroad, are mostly in a ruined and decayed condition, and in fact, the last and only large importation is a mass of decay and rubbish, not worth lhe freight.

From the New York Spectator , February 12. A portion of the Londoners were thrown into a state of considerable alarm, Jan. Gth, by the escape of a royal tiger from the menageris at Limehouse. He was seen leisurely marching down the Commercial road, in the dusk of the evening, the pedestrians of course giving him plenty of room for his parade, until he met a large dog, upon which he laid violent paws, without ceremony. Finally, perceiving a gate open, he walked into the yard, with the body of the dog. which he proceeded to devour, and while so engaged was secured, with no little difficulty. He was walking about his grounds, very early in the morning, with his steward, pointing out some trees which he meant to have cut down, when a shot was fired at him from the other side oi a hedge, which caused his death in a few hours. Six slugs were found to have pierced his side and breast, the largest passing through his lungs. The steward saw the murderer run away. (From the London Standard, Feb. 5.) The business of the second session of Parliament during the reign of her present Majesty was opened to-day by a speech from the throne. Shortly before two þÿo clock a discharge of cannon announced that her Majesty, accompanied by the great officers of state and the household, had left the Palace, and was proceeding to the House of Lords. The line through which the procession passed was lined vvirh two regiments of the Guards. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Queen arrived at the House of Lords about 2 o'clock, which was announced by a discharge of cannon Shortly afterwards her Majesty attended by the great officers of state entered the house, and took her seat on the throne The foreign ambassadors wore the full costumes of the countries they repre- . sented. Her Majesty having directed their lordships lo be seated. The Lord Chancellor directed the Usher of the Black Rod to summon the Commons to hpar her þÿMajesty speech s on the opening ol Parliament. In a few minutes the Commons appeared at the bar, headed bv the Speaker. The space below the bar was crowded with members þÿ After silence had been obtained, her Maje stv in a clear and audible voice read the following most gracious speech : þÿ THE QUEENS SPEECH. þÿ Mi/ Lords and Gentlemen, þÿ I rejoice to meet you again in Parliament I am particularly desirous of recurring to your advice and assistance at a period when many mutters of great importance demand your serious and deliberate attention. þÿ 1 continue to receive fiom Foreign Pow-

ers gratifying assurances of their desire to maintain with me the most friendly relations. þÿ 1 have concluded with the Emperor of Austria a treaty of commerce, which 1 trust will extend and improve the intercourse between my subjects and those of the Emperor. þÿ 1 have also concluded a treaty of the same kind with the Sultan, calculated to place the commercial relations between my dominions and the Turkish empire upon a better and more secure footing þÿ I have directed copies of these treaties to be laid before you. þÿ 1 have been engaged, in concert with Austria, France, Prussia and Russia, in negotiations with a view to a final settlement ol the differences between Holland and Belgium. þÿ A definitive treaty of peace, founded upon anterior arrangements which have been acceded to by both parties, has in consequence been proposed to the Dutch and Belgian governments. I have the satisfaction to inform you that the Dutch government has already signified to the Conference its acceptance of that treaty, and 1 trust that a similar announcement from the Belgian government will put an end to that disquietude which the present unsettled state of these affairs has necessarily produced. The unanimity of the five allied powers affords a satisfactory security for the preservation of peace. þÿ I lament the conlinuence of the civil war in Spain, which engages my anxious and undiminished attention. þÿ Differences which have arisen have occasioned the retirement of my minister from

Teherant. 1 indulge, however, the hope of learning that a satisfactory adjustment of these differences will allow of the re-establishment of my relations with Persia upon their former looting of friendship þÿ Events connected with the same differences have induced ihe Governor General of India to take measures for protecting British interests in that quarter of the world, and to enter into engagements, the fulfilment of which may render military operations necessary. For- this purpose such preparations have been made as may be sufficient to resist aggression from any quarter, dominions. the integrity ol my eastern and to maintain

bv acts of the colonial legislature, and that the transition from the temporary system ot apprenticeship to entire freedom has taken place without any disturbance of public order and tranquility. Any measures w hich may be necessary in order to give full effect to tins great and beneficial change will, I have no doubt, receive your careful attention. þÿ I have to acquaint you, with deep concern that the province of Lower Canada has again been disturbed by insurrection, and that hostile incursions have been made into Upper Canada by certain lawless inhabitants of the United States of North America. These violations of the public peace have been promptly suppressed by the valor of my forces and the loyalty of my Canadian subjects The president of the United States has called upon the citizens of the Union to abstain from proceedings incompatible vviih the friendly relations which subsist between Great Britain and the United States. þÿ I have directed full information upon all these matters to be laid before you. and 1 recommend the present state of these provinces to your serious consideration. 1 rely upon you to support my firm determination to maintain the authority of my Grow n, and I trust that your wisdom will adopt such measures as will secure to those parts of my empire, the benefit of internal tranquility, and the full advantages of their own great national resources. þÿ have 1 observed with pain the persevering efforts which have been made in some parts ot the country to excite mv subjects to diso-

bedience and resistance to the law, and to recommend dangerous and illegal practices For the counteraction of all such designs 1 depend upon the efficacy of the law, which it will be my duty to enforce, upon the good sense and right disposition of my people, upon their attachment to the principles of justice, and their abhorrence of violence and disorder. þÿ 1 confidently commit all these great interests to your wisdom, and I implore Almigh- þÿ ty God lo assist and prosper your counsels

Cut off by a verv short illness. Death brought with ii no ordinary pangs to the bosoms of bis children and some few particular friends, most particularly so to one þÿendear t d o him, by a succession of very many years in friendly intercourse and pleasing conversations. This melancholy event opened wounds, which time itself with its soothing influence, can never entirely heal. He has gone through deaths sleep unto þÿGod the affectionate Parent, the best of Friends and an Honest Man þÿ ( Communicated)

Mr. Editor.- Will you permit a stranger, who without having any personal mt' rest at stake, is influenced bv a strong desire to render some return for the uniform kiudrw ssatid hospitality which has been extended to himself and other visitors, by the gentlemen ol litis Island lo enquire thro' the columns ol your pi'f-er- " Why do the planters permit the opportunity for reaping golden harvests from the silk cultivation, to pass bv unimproved It cannot arise from want of courage and enterprise lor the successful exploration ot new avenues of gain. It is undoubtedly attributable to a want of attention to the subject ; and to ibat caution which restrains from action on subjects with w hich we are not familiar But such caution is uncalled for here, because the si'.k cultivation is not to be regarded in the light of a doubtful experiment ; for it has been in successful progress, and a source ot wealth to other countries, for hundreds of years Its practicability here, is the principle thing that has escaped attention ; and the promise of such enormous pecuniary returns fioin rearing the Mulbcrrv. in consequence of the adaptedness of the climate and tiie abundance ol laborers, seein to have been disregarded. Besides, the ex pence of ari experiment is so trilling, that that caution, which prevents our acting on such a subject, becomes folly. Upon investigation, an almost incredible mass of facts will be discovered ; and I would respectfully refer those of vour readers to whom the subject is

not familiar, to their Encyclopedia's, or to anv of the various modern publications on the silk culture, in proof ot my assertion. In the United States, where the population are not in the habit of distrusting any enterprise merely because tliev never appreciated its advantages before, thousands there entered into the business, and are laying the foundation for rich returns, while many have already realized great wealth from it In many ol the West India Islands, the planters are sedulously engaging in cultivating the Mulberry, for the production of silk, and most ol them, strange as it may seem, could more easily be persuaded to abandon the cultivation oi the cane, than of the mulberry. In this Island several enterprising gentlemen, as 1 am informed, have supplied themselves with the Morus Multicaulis, the best Mulberrytree known. A gentleman of the highest respectability has informed the writer that in Montserrat they have ascertained that one acre of the Mulberry will yield leaves sufficient to produce silk to the value of Eighty Pounds Sterling, Q' or about Three Hundred r ( Fifty Dollars ! This is no surprising estimate to those who understand the subject. Regarded as an estimate for any one Y ear, it falls short of the truth; for at least three crops of leaves can he secured annually, which will make the product $1050 00 pr acre pr annum. Besides, the cultivation of the Mulberry will not interfere with that of the cane ; the expences will be trifling compared with the lat-

ter ; and the small children can labor at this business to as great advantage as adults. Let your readers calculate the great results tor themselves; and let them not be prevented from trying the business (on a small scale, if they please) for themselves, by astonishment and incredulity at the results. On this subject, the enterprising proprietor of Montpellier estate can afford muck valuable practical information, if 1 may take the liberty thus publicly to refer to him ; which 1 do the more freely, from knowing his strong desire to see his neighbors profiting from the Mulberry cultivation ; and because he has established, for his own use, a Nursery of the Morus Multicaulis, intending soon to ship the surplus to New York, where be they in great. Cash demand. No doubt would are prefer to have them scattered thro' the Island, ultho' in a pecuniary point of view it can be of no interest to him. I hope the inhabitants will not permit one of these trees to leave the Island ; but, as some have already done, take immediate measures to supply themselves with 1000 or more, with which tocomnieuce; and from them rear Millions to enrich themselves, and leave a source of profitable income to their cluldrcn. A Saw Votuoji.

Government intend þÿ not directly from themselves, but through a confidential supporter in the commons þÿ to propose that wheat shall be imported at a fixed duty of 10s per quarter for the first year ; 9s for the second ; 8s. for the third : 7s for the fourth ; 6s. for the fifth ; and 5s. for the sixth year, after the law has passed ; and then have a permanent fixed duty of 5s. per quarter." From the 'St. James Chronicle' Feb. 14. NEWS FROM INDIA. The retirement of Sir H. Fane from the command of the army had been announced in general orders. 1-our thousand more troops from Bombay were to be sent to Sir John Keane. fhe troops for Aden were embarked fiom Bombay on the 30th December. The following is an extract of a letter from an officer on the Bengal establishment who is well acquainted with India, dated the 7th of November " The army of Candahar, as it is called, consisting of about 15,000 men, has assembled at Kernaul, and will march about the first proximo to Ferozepore, on the banks of the Sutlej, where Lord Auckland will have an interview with Kunjcet Singh, and, it is said, endeavour to persuade him to allow our forces to pass through his dominions. Should he refuse, they will descend to Shikarpoorc. on the Indus, thence to Caudahar, where the first opposition will be met, and finally to Cabul or Heart, as circumstances may require. It is, however, the opinion of ntariv that there will be little bloodshed unless the Russian really give their assistance to our enemies. Nevertheless, I believe, since India came under our dominion, she has never

been so threatened and in such a da gerous position as at present. All the independent native powers by whom we are surrounded are collecting their forces and strengthening their positions, and there is no doubt thai ilie slightest reverse to onr arms in the north would bring them upon us. From the New York Commercial Advertiser March 12, 1839. For the Commercial Advertiser. There appears to me to be, in the public mind, a very great misapprehension of the border difficulties. If 1 rightly understand the matter, the King of Holland, in the compromise which he offered for the acceptance of the United States and Great Britain, gives us all the disputed territory where the border war is now in prospect, up to the river St. Johns; and to Great Britain, all the land North of the bend of the St. Johns and its tributaries. As an equivalent for this territory, so necessary to Britain and so useless to us, it awards to us House's Point, on I.ake Champlain, with a stiip of land three miles wide, extending from the Lake to the St. Lawrence. This would extend the Northern boundary of the state of New York three miles farther North, For my own part, I think this is a fair equivalent. The United States would doubtless be willing to pav to Maine #3(10.000 for the point and fort, and probably the fee simple of the land would sell for as much as the land awarded to Britain, ( if we include the value of the point and fort ; and if not, the general government had bolter make it up than involve the country in war. Now those who want to bringon war. represent that one third part of the territory of Maine is claimed by Britan, and say that if we allow them this claim, they will serve us as we served the Indians, and claim still moie untill they get the whole of Maine. This is, I believe, a false representation. Britain offers to give us up the whole seat of the war, up

to the river St. Johns, and House's Point, and the strip of land into the bargain, if Maine will relinquish that part of the claimed territory which lies North of the St. þÿJohns. The whole dispute then is for the right of sovereignty over this small corner. Whether the government of New- Brunsw ick shall support the paupers, and punish the felons, or the state of Maine. As to their trade, it would all go to Quebec on one side and St. Johns on the other, let who will have the sovereignty, and their political influence, as it might happen. MODERATOR.

flMMMUlflMhaMMMj FROM THE EAST The provincial papers talk quite as nonsenicallv about the present condition and fu. ture prospects of matters relating to the dispute, as any of our þÿown the slang-whangers on both sides appearing to think it. a point high necessity to profess the utmost of contempt for each other, individually and nationally The advices from Houlton are of the 6th, evening. Nothing new. The Maine papers and letters persist in declaring that the 11th legiment had arrived at Madawaska on the 4th, when we know that the two advance companies only reached Quebec on that day, from Sorel, on their way to New Brunswick. The positive manner in which this erroneous statement is made, throws doubt on all the reports front New Brunswick that come to us by the way of Maine. From Bangor the only news we have is that, on the 8th, six companies ol the Kennebec detachment, or division, took up the line of march for Houlton. From Augusta we have intelligence dated the 9ih. t)n the 7th General Scott visited Governor Fairfield at the Council Chamber, and subsequently was introduced to the Hepresentatives in their hall He was addressed by E. H. Allen Esqr. of Bangor, and made one of his usual neat replies. On the 8tl> Governor Fairfield reviewed the detachments from Cumberland and Oxford ; about 1000 strong.

I ROM IV E W-BRUISS H ICK. Late from Fuedeuicton. þÿ There is no truth in the statement that the militia had been ordered from Fredericton, to the disputed territory. They were on Tuesday last performing garrison duty at head quarters. Stephen Miller, Esq. who had been sent by His Excellency Sir John Harvey, with despatches to the Governor General, was expected to return to Fredericton on Tuesday or Wednesday þÿnext. The Hon. A. E. Botsford, who it will be recollected was sent by His Excellency with despatches to Washington, was expected in Fredericton next week. Below we give the spirited address of Col. Maxwell, of the 36th Hegt. to a few companies of the 1st Battalion Carleton Militia. The promptness with which our militia volunteered their services to protect their country from a hostile invasion, and the enthusiasm with which the address was received, fully warranted the gallant colonel in declaring that he had come among the right stuff. Men of New Brunswick, and Militia of the County of Carleton! 1 have had the high honor of being sent here by your distinguished and talented Governor to assume the command of this district, and proud I feel of this commission, for I know I have come amongst the right stuff for your fame has spread far and wide as good þÿwoodsmen good þÿmarksmen and gallant warriors: and your devotion and loyalty to your Queen and your mother country and your fatherland, is unequalled. Circumstances may oblige me in a day or two to call for your active services in the

field, when 1 feel assured that all I have heard of you will be fully realized ; for I know you have all the attributes of soldiers, and that my duty will be more to repress than to stimulate you, should the occasion 'arrive when you are obliged to quit your own lire sides,

which your daring spirit makes you so prompt to defend from encroachment. You will again prove what 1 have so often heard of the New Brunswickers, that they have bodies of adamant and souls of fire ! and that they have the material within them for making the best soldiers in the known world ! Having said this much, I have only to remind you that the first qualities of the soldier, are good þÿconduct þÿsteadiness and obedience to his superiors. Your colonel has informed me, as well as Major Dibble, who is placed in the immediate command of you þÿ and whom 1 am proud to have under my orders þÿ that your zeal and alacrity in your country's cause is such, that you have volunteered to assemble to receive lessons in the military art, before you are regularly called out. I have therefore directed my adjutant and sergeant major to give you the first rudiments of a profession that 1 am sure you might do honor to, at such time and place as may be most convenient to all parties.

From the New l ock Commercial Advertiser, March 23. FROM MAINE. The Eastern advices continue to be of a pacific character, the war fever having ceased to rage, apparently, every where but in the House of Assembly. We give such extracts from the Boston papers as have any interest. Correspondence of the Boston Morning Post. Augusta, March 19, 1839. þÿ "Grim visaged warhath smoothed herwrinkled front' a little, of late, in this quarter. The aspect of affairs touching the N. E. boundary dispute, is not altogether so bellicose as it seemed to be a few weeks since. Things however remain nearly in stat. Our troops retain peaceable and undisputed possession of the Aroostook country, while Sir John Harvey contents himself with the occupation of the Tobiquc (within her Majesty's unquestioned dominions) by a military force of about 125 men. He has also, it is said, two regiments quartered at another point lower down. The resolution which passed the Senate, (authorising the Governor to withdraw the forces whenever satisfied that no hostile movements are to be apprehended from New Brunswick.) was still under discussion in the House. Various amendments had been proposed by gentlemen who had war speeches on hand, and wanted to deliver them. Mr. Delesdernier moved to amend so as to provide that the military force shall not be withdrawn, until the Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick shall have abandoned his claim of jurisdiction over the disputed territory. This was debated one whole day ; and on the next Mr Delcsdernier withdrew it, and offered another,

in the words following, to wit : þÿ Resolved, That the right of this state to exclusive jurisdiction over all that territory claimed by Great Britain, which lies west of the line due north from the monument to the north-west angle of Nova Scotia, (usually denominated the disputed territory,) has been constant and indefeasible since her existence as an independent state ; and no agreement which has or may be entered into by the Government of the Union, can impair her prerogative to be the sole judge of the time when, and the manner in which, that right shall be enforced.

Resolved, That this state, in view of the measures recently adopted by the Government of the Union in relation to this question, and particularly the provisions made for a special minister to the Court of St. James; and actuated by an earnest desire to come to an amicable adjustment of the whole controversy, will forbear to enforce her jurisdiction in that part of her territory, the possession of which is now usurped by the province of New Brunswick, so far as she can do consistently with the maintenance of the resolve of the 24th January last þÿ but she has seen nothing in recent events to cause her to doubt that it is her imperative duty, as well as her invariable right, to protect her public domain from depredation and plunder up to the exlimits of her territory, and that no power on earth shall drive her from an act of ders. It is probable that the re- i jurisdiction, so proper in itself, and to which her honor is so irrevocably committed. Resolved, That the public measures of the Governor of this state, in relation to the dis. puted territory, meet the cordial approbation of this Legislature ; that they concur in the doctrines and sentiments contained in his recent message ; that they will sustain him in carrying « o into effect the resolve of the 24th January aforesaid; and that whenever he shall be fully satisfied, by the declarations of the Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick or otherwise, that the latter has abandoned all intentions of occupying the disputed territory

with a military force, and of attempting the expulsion of our party, that the exigency which called for the military having ceased, the Governor be, and he hereby is authorized to withdraw the same, leaving the laud agent with a sufficient posse, armed or unarmed, as the case may require, to carry said resolve into effect Mr. Vose offered the following, as additional to the resolutions of Mr. Delesdernier. Resolved. That as the practicability of running and marking the North Eastern boundary line, in accordance with tiie provisions of the treaty of 1783, is indubitable þÿ to consent to another arbitration, in pursuance of the recommendation of the President of the United States, would be a virtual abondonment of the rights and interest of Maine. Resolved, That a crisis has arrived when it becomes the duty of the General Government forthwith to propose to the Government of Great Britain a joint commission for the purpose of running the line in accordance with the treaty of 1783 þÿ and in case of a refusal on the part of Great Britain, it is the duty of the United States to run the line upon her own authority, and to take possession of the whole disputed territory without unnecessary delay. All these were adopted, in committee of the whole yeas 165, nay 1. And thus the matter stood on the 20th, which is the date of our latest from Augusta.

From the London Times, February 27. 1839. Our advices from Brussels come down to the evening of Sunday. Everything remained perfectly quiet, awaiting the report of the Chambers, which it was expected would be made on the following day or Tuesday. The Chamber of Commerce of this city had voted unanimously the following address to the Chamber of Representatives : þÿ þÿ 'Gentlemen, þÿ You are at this moment called upon to bring to a conclusion the political differences which have so long existed between Holland and Belgium, and to vote on the project of a treaty agreed to by the j conference of London. þÿ This project cuts off from the Belgian territory several portions of the provinces of Luxemburg and Limburg. We deplore that this painful sacrifice j should be imposed on our country, and if we i thought that in resisting this abuse of strength we could prevent our compatriots from being separated from Belgium, we should be ready to devote ourselves to their defence. But the j live great Powers of Europe have declared their will : it is irrevocable. Resistance would bring upon our country the greatest evils, and compromise its nationality. þÿ 1 You would not, gentlemen, wish to take upon yourselves the responsibility of a war, in which the blood of our brave youth would he spilt without a hope of success, and which would involve the complete rule of our industry and commerce. þÿ Already, Gentlemen, we are bound to declare it to you, the country has suffered immense losses, and the private misfortunes which have occurred are only indication of

the much greater, the much deeper evil, by I which every branch of commerce has been, and continues to be, affected. An adjournment of the question which occupies you would increase the evil a hundredfold, and finish by destroying all confidence ; to pro. lone the sufferings of the country is become j impossible. þÿ þÿ The Chamber of Commerce of Brussels in conjuring you, gentlemen, to bow to necessity, and to adoot the project of law presented to you by the Government, is convinced that it expresses the wishes of all who are interested tn the public prosperity and the national welfare. " þÿ We be<r of vou to receive the assuran- i ces of our þÿrespect, See. þÿ The Chamber of Commerce of Liege has also voted a petition in favour of the adoption of the þÿtreaty.

The following passage in our Paris letter goes> I 1839. however, if wellfounded, to settle this question very differently : þÿ þÿ 1 have taken all the steps practicable to arrive at a probable guess at the result of the impending elections, and find that the general opinion is that Ministers will he in a minority in the new Chamber. A letter from Toulon, dated the 20th inst., published in the Paris papers of Monday, showed that the late contradiction given by the Moniteur to the rumoured intention of Government to send land forces to Mexico was equivocal and evasive It appears from the letter in question that the Jupiter ship-ofthe line and the Thetis frigate were positively under orders to take troops on board for that destination. From the Morning Courier and New York Enquirer, March 30, 1839. Mexico. þÿ The British sloop of war, Modeste, of 18 guns, from Vera Cruz and the Havana, arrived here yesterday Her commander, Gapt Eyres, 11. N , has given to our ship news reporter a confirmation of the account published by us yesterday, that a treaty of peace had been concluded between the h rench Admiral and the representatives of the Mexican Government. IMPORTANT FROM þÿMEXICO By the Dromo, Capt. How, arrived yesleiday from Havana, we have received a file of the Diario de la Habaua to the 18th instant. From the paper of that date, we translate the following important news : þÿ letters from Vera Cruz of the 10th By March, we learn that a treaty has been concluded between Don Edward de Corosteza and General Victoria on the part of Mexico and Admiral Baudin on the part of France, the British Minister, Mr Packenham acting as mediator, of the following tenor : þÿ 1st. There shall be an armistice of fifteen days. 2nd. The Mexicans shall pay 000,000 dollars in periods ot 2, 4 and 0 months. 3rd. Indemnification for the expenses of the war and to the expelled Frenchmen, shall be finally settled by a nation in friendship with the two contracting parties. 4th. The Casile ol St. J. Ulloa shall be delivered up to the Mexicans as soon as it shall be known that the treaty has been ratified by þÿCongress. The same letters say that there was no doubt the treaty would be immediately ratified. Mr Gorostiza had set of) to the city of Mexico to remove any dilficultics that might

<rasTag©J3E present themselves. In the meantime the discharge ol all vessels of all classes and nations was allowed VeraCruz will again receive within her walls the persons who have emigrated, and the 11th will open to the merchants their former places of þÿbusiness. The above intelligence is confirmed by Captain How, who states that the British frigate Medea. Commodore Douglass, and the British sloop of war Race Horse, had arrived at Havana from Vera Cruz, with letters to the above effect, and would proceed immediately to England.

Sir: I have the happiness to enclose here with two copies þÿol the arrangement entered into through my agency, between the Governor of Maine and the Lieutenant Governor of the Province of New Brunswick. The copy of my official note to Sir John Harvey, with his acceptance of the arrangement, is iu the hands of the Governor of Maine, and another copy of the same official note, followed by the acceptances of the Lieutenant Governor and the Governor, was yesterday transmitted by me to Sir John Harvey At the same time 1 sent him copies of two orders which were yesterday issued by the Governor ol Maine þÿ theirs/ disbanding the thousand detached nnlitia which has been held in reserve at this place, and the second recalling the military lorce of the Slates limn the disputed temloi y ; and directing the organization of the civil posse, that is to be held by the State in that territory. The papers so transmitted, and which bore the signature of the Governor of Maine, or that of Ins Adjutant General, were officially certified by me. 1 trust that the arrangement between the Governor and Lieutenant Governor, together with my humble agency, in bringing it about, will be satisfactory to the President and the Department. I'he arrangement, 1 have no douol, will be executed by the parlies to it in good tdith and iri cheerfulness. Mv Dear General Scott: Upon my return from closing the session of ihe Provincial Legisiatuie this day, 1 was gratified by the receipt of your veiy satisfactory communications of the 2 1st instant. £.T33» From the London Morning Post Thursday March 14, 1839, The extracts from the New York end other American papers, received by the Great Western, which appear in our paper this day, present some additional details connected with the threatened collision between the forces ol the State of Maine and those ul the British province of New Brunswick. It is impossible not to perceive in the facts as they are detailed by the Governor ot Maine himself to the Legislature of that State, and in the hostile resolutions adopted by the latter with promptitude and unanimity, upon the Governor's representations, that in this part of the Union a settled purpose exists to take forcible possession of the disputed territory, at the risk, or, more probably, with the view, of exciting a war beiween Great Britain and tiie American Federation. To w hat extent the hostile feelings and intentions of the population of Maine may be diffusi d among other portions of the people of the United States, and how far tins pugnacious disposition may be encouraged or repressed by tiie General Government, remains yet to be seen. Much light upon ti.e latter question, and, indeed, upon the former also- for popularity must always he the aim, and popular feeling the guide, of the American Gov. þÿeminent ill re alfi'i led Iv the Message upon the : of affairs In the disputed territory which the President via- expected to communicate to Congress .on the 25'h ult., ami by the discussions in that Assembly which must spring from it. In 'he m anwhile, the determined hostility towards Great Bri-

tain of at least one State of the American Union, that State being its own nearest neighbour, is placed beyond doubt by the clearest evidence of facts. The people and the Government of Great Britain will fall into a great and dangerous error if they do not prepare themselves for all the consequenceswhich such a disposition as we have described in such a quarter may produce. It is well that we have a considerable military force in North America at the present moment, and that the Canadian rebels are, at least for the present, effectually put clown. It behoves the British Government indeed to consider whether our army in North America, considerable as it is ought not as speeuily as possible to be reinforced.

Since the Ministry "f the 15th of April, says our Gallic contemporary, ' the Kino often presides at the Council lie appears to tie more .Minister than his Ministers, and seems to lie the verv soul of his .Ministry. which cannot deliberate freely before the Kino. It is known by each one that the Royal word must pass with the majority. The Kino makes and unmakes the Ministers? who would therefore dare to contradict him and resist his will In England the King is very seldom present at the Cabinet Councils. It is always by the First Lord of the Treasury that the thoughts of Royalty are transmitted to the Ministers. Casimir I'erier, who at least had the merit of desiring a really constitutional Government., assembled the whole of the Ministers around him, and by thus doing he really represented the ideas of the Government. In his lifetime responsibility was not extended beyond the Ministry ; and this is the principle which must again he enforced. The elections have terminated against the Government of the Court, and the first act of the pew Ministry must he to annul that occult and dangerous power. When the Kino governs the courtiers are masters, and Ministers count for nothing. Let the Cabinet deliberate under the real Presidency of a responsible Minister; let Ministers cease to assemble in presence of tiie Sovereign, and through the mere force of circumstances we shall have a Constitutional Government "

MONEY MARKET and CITY NEWS. City, Wednesday Evening. The intelligence received to-day from the United States has necessarily led to much discussion among our commercial men ; but however threatning the aspect of political affairs may have been in that direction at the time of the Great Western's departure, a very general hope seems still to be entertained that the peace of ihe two nations may not be disturbed. There can lie no doubt whatever that the American Government will do all in their power to restrain their citizens on the border from further acts of violence against the authority of this country. Their ability or inability to carry their wishes into effect is another & a more important question. Upon this point there must necessarily be much uneasiness. The districts of the Union contiguous to the British possessions are extremely populous, arid, as the numbers increase, the impatience of the majority of them to extend their occupation of territory towards the north east becomes more and more manifest The funds have felt the influence of this unwelcome intelligence from America, as will be seen bv our quotations, though not to so great and extent as might have been expected.

St. roix Christian sled 6tli May, 1839. The mail pr: first April Packet reached us on Saturday 4th inst. She must have had a very fine run to Barbados. London dates of the 1st April are received by her. Parliament had adjourned over the Easter holy days þÿ the motion to enquire into the Corn Laws having been thrown out by a large majority in the House of Commons (196 yeas to 342 nays) notwithstanding three of the ministers voted in the affirmative, it had excited much discontent among the working classes, particularly the manufacturers. The people were arming, and detachments of the regular troops were marching into the disaffected districts. One third of the militia had been call'd into service by the Government. þÿ Lord John Russell's motion to take the sense of the House of Commons on the administration of the Government in Ireland, was to be debated on the 15th April ; þÿ should there be a majority, (as in the Lords,) against approving the conciliatory system adopted bv the Marquis of Normanby, ministers will resign. The negotiation regarding the Boundary question with the If. States is said to be transferred from London to Washington. In France the King hf.d not yet been able to fix the new ministry. Thiers, to whom he gave a Carte Blanche, refuses to take office unless Soult is at the head of the new ministry, while it is said, the latter will not accept office on the condition® (relative to Spain), prescribed by Thiers. In the mean time the King has again prorogued the Chambers. þÿ The Legislative Body of Belgium have at

last consented to ratify the treaty of the 24 articles, by which their long standing dispute with Holland is brought to a close. The John Bull of March 31st says that Lord Melbourne is to be married to the Duchess of Kent (mother of the Queen) in June ! þÿ the former is sixty and the latter finy three years of age. From the. Neu) York Emigrant and Old Countryman, April 17, 1839.

Bv the Steam Ship Great Western, Capt. Husken, from Bristol, we have London dates to the 22d ult. The Western has had a longer passage than usual, occasioned by the Strong westerly gales which she has had to encounter during all the voyage, except the last two days. She sailed from Bristol on the 23d ult., and arrived at Sandy Hook about midnight of the 13th inst., with 109 passengers. The Liverpool Steam Ship had not arrived at the time of the Western's departure, but the England Packet Ship had brought to Liverpool the President's message on the subject of the North Eastern Boundary, together with the recommendation of Messrs. Fox and Forsyth to Sir John Harvey and Gov. Fairfield, for the suspension of hostilities, as detailed formerly. This account of things has been received in New York with apparently great satisfaction, and Stocks rose immediately full 3 per cent. : it seems, therefore, that apprehensions of war between the two countries, are, for the present, allayed. We have formerly stated the issue of Mr. Villier's motion in the House of Commons, for allowing the examination of witnesses at the Bar of the House, relative to the operation of the corn laws. The honorable member, believing the sense of the House to be not fully expressed, through such a medium, brought forward another motion for the appointment of a committee of the whole house, to take these laws into consideration. This produced an animated and lengthened discussion of five nights, at the termination of which

the motion of Mr. Villiers was negatived, upon a division, by a vote of 342 to 195. This may be said to have decided the fate of the Corn question during the present session. One of the most important debates in the present session of Parliament, is that arising from a motion of the Earl of Koden, for the appointment of a committee to inquire into the state of crime, and the administration of justice, in Ireland. On that evening, in the House of Commons Lord John Russell said that if a similar vote should take place in the House of Commons, that he and his colleagues would resign the government into other hands. We subjoin his remarks, in which he gave notice that he should speedily submit a motion to the House which should call for an expression of opinion on the policy of the government towards Ireland, which had been pursued for the last few years. " Lord J. RUSSELL said he wished, before proceeding with the Committee of Supply, to postpone several orders that stood on the paper, and in moving the postponement of the committe on the Irish Municipal Cor. poration Bill under the 1 5th of April, he w ished to state to the House the intentions of government. It was his intention, in the first week after the recess, on one of the first days after the house met, to ask the opinion of the House as to the government of Ireland during the last few years. Hear.J It appeared from a minute of the proceedings in the House ol Lords, that Inst night, or rather early this morning, that House agreed to ap-
point a select committee to inquire into the state of crime and outrages in Ireland since the year 1835. Hear. Now, without entering into the argument as to whether that

JBASTSJE T33Tawxasx inquiry was a proper one or not, it must be obvious to all, that fixing the year 1835 as the date of inquiry into crime and outrage, there must be a general belief throughout the empire, and more especially in that part to which it referred, that it was intended the inquiry should be conducted by one branch of the legislature only and confined to one administration. There was another point of importance, too, in the proposed inquiry, and that was, it trenched upon one of the highest prerogatives of the Crown, viz, the prerogative of mercy. Hear He did not say that there was not arguments to justify the House of Lords in taking such a course, but they were arguments which might not, perhaps, convince the House of Commons ; and this he would say, that no person could possibly be found to carry on the Government of Ireland with safety and satisfaction, unless he was assured that he possessed the confidence of the House of Commons. It was absolutely necessary to know whether that House would sanction the principle of inquiry, limited to the year 1835, as now entertained. The Noble Lord proceeded to say that in accordance with Lord Melbourne's often expressed declaration that he would hold office as long as he continued to possess confidence of the House of Commons hear, hear, it w is incumbent upon him Lord J. Russell) to bring that question at the earliest possible moment to an issue. Hear, hear He should ask the House whether they adhered to trie principles on which the government of

Ireland had of late been conducted. Hear, hear lie was perfectly aware that, as a government, the present administration had not been abie to carry all those bills which they had deemed it advisable to introduce hear, hear but they had been able, with the confidence of the llo use of Commons, and the forbearance of the other House, hear to carry on the administration in Ireland in a manner, he thought, conducive to the safety and advantage of that country. Wear lie should, therefore, call upon the House of Commons to say whether Lord Ebruigton was to continue the same line of policy as his predecessor, /fear. It was only fair to the Noble Lord that anexpression should be given on the subject, ffcar If the House should be of opinion that a different line of policy in the administration of Ireland ought to be introduced, then, said the Stable Lord, we shall relinquish into other hands the Government oj this country " Loud cries of f/ear, hear from all sides.

The system adopted by the present administration has been that of conciliation, and, backed as they are by Mr. O'Connell and his friends, it is probable that ministers will carry a majority, when the point shall be mooted in the commons.

Steam conveyance to America. þÿ Government have entered into a contract for conveying the mails, by large and powerful steamvessels, from Liverpool to Halifax, and thence by branch steamers to Boston, and in the summer to Quebec. The mercantile interests, not only in the North American colonies, but also in the United States, will be gratified to learn that, instead of a monthly communication as formerly, steamers will now be despatched on the 1st and 15th of each month. The enterprising contractor has engaged with those ableuud scientific builders, Messrs

A'TJS. Wood, at Port Glasgow, to build three ships of 1.009 tons each, in which Robert Napier, Esq., is to place engines of 400 horse power. London. March 21. þÿ State of the Country. þÿ A large body ol' artillery marched yesterday from Woolwich into Northamptonshire. The object is, doubtless, the prevention of outrage in the manufacturing districts. In reply to a question put bv admitted ingham. Lord Melbourne the Duke of Buck- a few days ago, that government was cognizant of the fact, that the Chartists throughout the kingdom are arming by thousands. The times are such as to require on the part of the executive, a large measure of wisdom, promptitude, and firmness. Departure of the Lord-Lieutenant for Ireþÿland. On the 19 th March, Her Majesty's armed steamer Meteor. Lieutenant-Commander R 14. Pritchard, left Woolwich dockyard, having taken on board the baggage, plate, and part of the suite of his Excellency the newlv appointed Lord Lieutenant ol Ireland, the Right Hon. Baron Fortescue, K P., who will embark at Plymouth (he being on a visit to his venerable parent, Earl Fort scue, in Devonshire,) after this beautiful and commodious steam vessel has touched at Portsmouth. The commander of this vessel is an old Trafalgar officer, and served on board Nelson's own ship the Yictorv and was severely wounded ; It is therefore expected after this trip he will receive a step of rank, this being t he second occasion on which the gallant office r has hoisted the Royal standard.

CANADA PRISONERS. From the London Gazette we learn the names and destinies of these prisoners. Eighteen of them are to be transported to a penal colony, and tbe other five to be released at the boundary line on Lake Ontario. Fourteen are yet remaining in the jail at London, who are to be kept a while longer and then liberated. The term of their detention will depend on the continuance of quiet on the frontier. The army of Sir John Keene was retreating, the Sindcs having assumed a decidedly hostile position. Captain Barnes, who had been sent forward reconnoitre, reported that the passes were all strongly fortified, and would be, as he judged, obstinately defended. The troops were suffering from want of Provisions and other necessaries, and it is stated that the loss ef men already amounted to 3,000, although ihev have not as yet encountered an enemy. The directors of the East India company are extremely urgent in their demands that the European army in India shall be reinforced to a great extent, and witii the utmost speed.

From the John Bull, London, March 31, 1839. T he following communication is from the Irisli correspondent of the Times : þÿ Dublin, March 25. agitation on a grand scale. þÿ arrival of mr. o'connell. The following manifesto appeared in the papers this morning, and Mr. U'Connell has arrived to continence the campaign of agitation sketched in this epistle. The Precursor Society has been summoned for to-morrow, when Mr. O'Connell will enter into a detail of his system of operations : þÿ " London , March 22, 1839. "My dear Kay, þÿ The people of Ireland will see with satisfaction the decided and manly part which the Ministry have resolved to adopt. They bring forward, on or about the 15th April, the question before the House of Commons þÿ shall Ireland continue to be governed on the wise, humane, and impartial principles acted on since 1835 by Lord Melbourne's Government, or shall she be handed over to the truculent, the furious, and the sanguinary Orange faction ? This question the House of Commons is to answer. The House of Lords have, consistently enough, chosen the worst part ; and under the guidance of that harsh and ungenerous old man, Wellington, declared for the Orange faction. There was a time when you would have been surprised to read the newspaper speech of Lord Brougham, yelping in with the vilest of the Orange rabble. But no one is now surprised anything unprincipled at so a statesman writes or sings, says or yelps. " Well, then, the tug of war is to come on the 15th of April. 1 intend to go to-morrow to Liverpool, and on Sunday night, unless it

blows a whole gale, to go to Dublin. If not on Sundav night, o ' then on that of Monday. J Reckon on me for Tuesday at the latest. " The fate of Ireland depends on Lord John's motion conciliation or oppression. þÿ þÿ There is time, however, for the Irish nation to speak out þÿ loud, long, and unanimous. I mean to move on Tuesday an address to the Irish people, calling on them to rally at once against the diabolical Orange faction, a faction enriched by the spoils and red with the blood of the Irish nation. Let us pteaceably, tranquilly, but at once meet, petition, and remonstrate. Let me present 300, 000 petitioners at the bar of the House of Commons, calling by their respectful but firm petitions on the British Legislature to avert from our lovely

green land the horror of civil war and blood1 shed ; and to continue to us at least a just, merciful, and impartial administration, until they grant us the equalisation of civil rights and religious freedom, which cannot be as long as the majority of the Irish people support the Church of the minority. " Hurrah for this peaceful conflict ! I like this straightforword boldness of the blow of the Ministry ; it is what we desire þÿ a collision between the two Houses on a great, a vital, and an important principle þÿ the principle on which Ireland is to be governed, either for a faction, or for the people. Hurrah for the Irish people I It makes me young again to engage in this conflict. All Ireland will, 1 trust, at once become ' Precursors.' It is the name of peace in which we will fight our bloodless battle. Hurrah for old Ireland ! " Circulate these tidings þÿ I will be with you to enforce these sentiments. " Faithfully yours, » DANIEL O'CONNELL. " To M. Ray, Esq."
TO THE PEOPLE OF IRELAND. " Hereditary boiidsmeo, know ye not. ' Who would be free, themselves must strike the blow

" Fellow Countrymen, þÿ One of those occasions has arrived which in former times were either thrown away by Irishmen or perverted to bad purposes, but for which they have lately shown themselves fitted, and have turned to the best advantage. A crisis has taken place in the affairs of Ireland which must result either in securing the continuance of a just and impartial Government, or in restoring the old sanguinary reign of blood-thirsty Orangeism, and filling the land once again with partiality, injustice, violence, and bloodshed. " Before the passing of the Reform Bill the Peers of Great Britain, with the aid of a few of the landed proprietors, held the Monarch in thraldom and the people in subjection ; the will of the aristocracy was the law of the land, and the House of Commons was controlled by a majority of the nominees of a few individuals. " The total object of the Reform Bill was to alter this unconstitutional state of thingSj and to give to the Commons' House of Parliament a salutary control over the other branches of the Legislature. To enable the Reform Bill to work well, the Ministry ought to have sought a contest and a collision with the House of Lords. They ought to have adopted such measures of amelioration, economy, legal and judicial and ecclesiastical improvements, as would have embodied the opinions of the wise and good in the British dominions þÿ compelled the House of Lords to yield to þÿ the popular sentiments, and, however reluctantly, to concur in perfecting all our institu-

tions. " These great purposes, however, would have required an Administration composed of men of energy and decision, as well as of talent and patriotism. " But, alas ! our leading men were unequal to the great occasion. With vixen forwardness they passed the first session oi the first Reform Bill in trampling upon Ireland, and binding her fast in the chains of Coercion Bills. Ireland had, however, her revenge, and the leading coercionists in the Ministry were flung aside by their own þÿcolleague.

Another Liberal Ministry was formed of | rather better materials, but who have altogeth er shrunk from the majestic duly imposed upon them. They have submitted to, and shrunk from, the usurpation of the Lords, and sought an inglorious peace by refusing to press for' ward, or even concur in. measures of eminent public utility, and, indeed, ol obvious necessity. " The rest of the empire had reason to com. plain; but Ireland had this singular advantage, that in the absence of legislative relie' she obtained administrative palliation of her evils. The Government of Ireland was conducted with mildness, lenity, and, above all, with perfect impartiality. The law was administered with vigour, but without partisan zeal. Official station was the reward of fitness and due capacity ; and to hate and depress the Irish people was no longer considered as the sole route to rauk and station. In short, Ireland was, for the first time in seven centuries, well and properly governed. Public affairs were no longer administered for the benefit of a virulent and blood-tbirstv faction, but were managed for the advantage of the nation at large. " This state of things was too good to be permitted to last. Accordingly the i'eels determined to resume their power, and, as a majority ot the House of Commons was favourable to the just and impartial administration of Irish affairs, the House of Lords determined to terminate the reign of Justice and impartiality in Ireland, and to restore the

hideous dominion of Orange corruption, partiality, and oppression. " That collision which the Ministry and the House of Commons shrunk from the Lords have boldiy proclaimed. " The ungenerous Wellington, who would be the bane ot his native land þÿ the unprincipled Brougham, the calamity of every party to which he has ever belonged þÿ have placed themselves at the head of the Orange menials, anil have proclaimed their determination to subvert the present Administration. 'I hey have attacked that Administration in its strongest point þÿ the Government of Ireland. " The Queen's .Ministers, on the other hand, have met this attack in the proper spirit þÿ they have not allowed the cry of collision from the Peers to pass unanswered. They, too, have proclaimed collision ; and the House ol Commons, in little more than a fortnight will have to decide whether the Lords are to become paramount in the Legislature, or whether, on the contrary, the House of Commons is to assume its proper attitude, at least on one subject, and to cheek the threatened and pressing despotism of the Lords. " If the Ministry succeed (as they ought, and we trust will), it will teach them a salutary lesson þÿ may they have the wisdom to learn and practise it ! þÿ it is this : þÿ That their safely as a Ministry, and, which is infinitely more, the safety of the Throne and nation, depend on their firmly, though cautiously, joining in the popular movement, and insisting upon ail those ameliorations which our

institutions require, and which the people, if once they were inspired with hope, would unanimously and irresistibly demand. " For the present, Ireland is the object of contention: Ireland is the battle field upon
Irishmen! it is our rights, our liberties, our properties, and our lives, that arc at stake. þÿ The great question is, whether we are to be governed in a spirit of fairness and impartiali-

" Irishmen ! lovers of peace and of constitutional liberty ! þÿ Irishmen ! who for so many years have pursued the paths of constitutional agitation, without violating any law of men, or, we trust, offending any ordinance of God þÿ Irishmen ! once more peaceably and firmly rally your country for and your Queen. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, April 17 18110. THE BOUNDARY QUESTION. We are enabled to state, on what we believe to be good authority, that such instructions have been transmitted to her Britannic Majesty's minister at Washington, by the Great Western, as will obviate the necessity of sending a special minister to London. The seat of negociations for the final adjustment ol the boundary question is transferred from London to Washington; and those negotiations will be pressed to a definitive conclusion. From the Observer. In the House of Commons on Friday night, Viscount Palinerslon. in answer to Sir Stratford Canning, expressed his confidence, with reference to the border disturbances between the state of Maine and New Brunswick, that the most friendly disposition was entertained by the American government toward this country, indeed, we have heard, from the most unquestionable authority, that the trespassers upon the disputed territory, arid whose conduct has provoked the threatened collision, are half citizens of the state of Maine itself, and half citizens of New Brunswick. It would most assuredly be absolute madness on the part of two governments such as that of the United States and of her Majesty, allied as they are by so many ties of common interest, to rush lino a general war on account of a bolder foray in which the subjects oi both arc equally implicated.

Mr. Papineau. þÿ The London and Paris papers received by the Great Western announces the arrival of Mr. Papineau at the latter city. The Paris correspondent of the American gives the following notice ot his reception and employment. Papineau has been favorably received in Paris by all the political parties. It is not true that he experienced at Havre any obstacle to bis coming hither. After the feasting of Louis Napoleon in England, even the Court party in France may be excused for investing a Papineau with some consequence, As the emancipation of the Canadas is deemed certain, sooner or later, the general French policy would seem to dictate that the refugee who can be considered as the representative of the French Canadian population, should be respectfully and kindly distinguished. He is understood to be already engaged in writing for the press a critical reply to Lord Durham's report on Canadian affairs. Such information and views as lie must be able to present, if skilfully exhibited, in a volume of moderate size, would probably circulate and make an impression, not merely in France, but over a large part of the European continent.
