From the New Orleans Bee, April 10. LATE AND HIGHLY IMPORTANT PROM MEXICO. By the arrival of the steam ship Meteor, from Vera Cruz, which place she left on the 2d inst., we have received the important and interesting information of the ratification of the treaty bv the Mexican government. Extract of a letter dated, ) Vera Cruz, April 2d, 1839. j " All the difficulties between Prance and Mexico have been terminated to mutual satisfaction. The conduct of Admiral Baudin during the whole course of hostilities has been highly praise worthy, and in the negotiations, while advancing the interests of France, he treated the Mexican government with the utmost deference þÿ and spared it even the shadow of any humiliation which might wound her amour proper. " Vera Cruz has resumed its activity. The confidence of the inhabitants in Admiral Baudin is such, that the debates in Congress having made them fear for awhile, that the treaty concluded by the plenipotentiaries at Vera Cruz, would not be entirely ratified, they were all determined to hoist the French flag, and place themselves under the protection of the Admiral. The ratification arrived, however, at last, on the 25th. It was full and satisfactory. " An imposing ceremony took place on the 27th, for the funeral services of the French who had died during the expedition." We are indebted to the polite attention of the French consul for the subjoined copy of the " order of the day," issued by Admiral f Baudin, upon receiving intelligence of the

treaty of peace between France and Mexico- ORDER OF THE DAY. Frigate Nekf-ide. ) Port of Vera Cruz, March 29, 1839. " The Admiral announces to the officers and soldiers of the squadron and garrison of Ulloa, that he has just received from the Mexican government, the ratification of the treaty of peace, concluded on the 0th of the month, between France and Mexico. The conditions were such as were required by the admiral. The cabinet of Mexico has abandoned the operation it intended carrying into effect ; the doubt which had arisen respecting the sincerity of the government have been j entirely dissipated. The Admiral, as the interpreter of the generous and benevolent intentions of France, has imposed very moderate conditions upon ! Mexico. The object of the expedition is, however, obtained. Mexico pays an indemnity of three millions of francs to those of our compatriots who had claims against her previous to the war. The necessary guarantees for the future j safety of the persons and property of the French, have been obtained. The amount of the indemnity to be paid to those who have suffered loss by the law of expulsion, shall be settled by arbitration. Our commerce in Mexico will lierealter he placed on the same footing as that of the most favored nations. In consequence of peace the fortress of Ulloa, will be restored to Mexico. This restitution will take place in the beginning of the ensuing month. The squadron will then return to France, with the exception of a few
vessels intended to remain in the neighborhood.

Sailors, rannonniers, miners, each of you in quitting the coast of Mexico, will feel the satisfaction of having co operated in a service useful and glorious to France The country against which you have fought, which you could have greatly injured, from which injury you have nevertheless abstained, will feel grateful for your moderation and your generosity. And your admiral will alwavs he happy to hear testimony to the spirit of order and subordination, the courage arid the devo tion you have exhibited throughout this expedition. Signed, CHARLES BAUDIN. A true copy þÿ The French Consul, DAVID. We learn that Admiral Baudin had signified to Mexico that if by the 20th March the ratification was not concluded, hostilities would re-commence. To this the Mexican government replied, that the ratification was in progress, hut that more time was required for its termination. The 27th was accordingly made the limits. The treaty arrived at Vera Cruz on the 25th. and was made known to the admiral at Antoin Lizadore the 27th.

We have received the following frem a correspondent, per steamer Hugh Lindsay: " ' ADEN, Jan. 30' " ' The fortified island of Liera and town of Aden, on the Arabian coast, in lat. 13 12 north, was stormed and captured on the 19th of January last by a force of European and Native Infantry, somewhat less than 1000 including artillery, commanded by Major Bailie, of the 24th Bombay Native Infantry, after it had been bombarded for two hours by the squadron commanded -by Captain Smith, R. N., consisting of her Majesty's frigate Volage, 28 guns, brig Cruiser, Commander King, 18 guns, lion Company's sloop ol war Coote, 18 guns, and schooner Inhye, 35 guns were taken, 27 of which were in battery ; 3 are very fine Turkish brass guns, 19, 17, and 16 feet long, 89, 85. and 68, pounders, which it is hoped will some of these days grace St. James's Park. The loss has been trifling on our part, and every thing seems quiet at present but the Arabs are a deceitful race, and it behoves the troops and their commander to be on the alert. It is understood that it has for some time past been the wish of government to obtain this stronghold, and negociations have been carried on for the last 15 months, but have constantly failed just as it was supposed all was concluded. The inhabitants seem delighted with the change of masters, particularly the Jews, who could never find favour in the eyes of their hard taskmasters."

BRUSSELS. March 27. " After four days of discussion, the Senate yesterday pronounced iu favoui of the treaty by a majority of 31 votes against 14. We bad hardly imagined to have found so large a majority in such an assembly. " At present, that the propositions of the Five Powers have been accepted, has Belgium nothing more to fear ? Is she sure of the quiet enjoyment of the rights which the Conference has been pleased to leave her ? þÿ Has she nothing left to do but to offer the kiss of peace to Holland? No! Many important questions are to be opened, as regards the debt, the navigation of the Scheldt, and of the mode of carrying into effect the treaty of the 23d of January. In these circumstances the national press has an immense duty to perform. " Never did a government more completely pledge itself than ours did to resistance by every means, or give assurance to its partisans of a firm and dignified policy. Warlike declarations, preparations for defence, adherence to an energetic system þÿ it did all that was in its power to persuade us that it was determined by every means to oppose the division of the Belgic territory; and, notwithstanding, it has proposed this division to the Chambers, it has constituted itself the advocate of the great powers, it has espoused their views with so much warmth, that one might imagine that it approved, nay shared them. ' Never did nation make so many protestations and demonstrations of every kind as Belgium against the 24 articles; never was

there such a hubbub and war-cry rung in the ears of Europe ; never did a people appear more unanimous in its projects of resistance and after all, the treaty, the object of all this resistance, has been adopted at Brussels.

SPAIN. The Madrid journals dated the 1 1th instant have arrived. No recent intelligence had been received from the Army of the North. The people were beginning to murmur at General Espartero's inaction, and loudly upbraided him for not profiting of the divisions in the Carlist camp to strike a decisive blow, and for having wasted without any results a sum of 40,000,000 reals, which the ministry forwarded to him during the months of January and February. Bayonnc letters of the 1 8th inst., state, that the impression was general in the north of

BMTSX. Tssrjtsnrjsx mxoraautsres Spain that the contest for the Spanish crown would he settled by treaty. The troops of Espartero and of Maroto respectively had returned to their quarters after a military promenade. An amelioration in the system of both leaders was perceptible. The Car. lists permitted the entry of the country people with their produce into the towns, and the Christines tolerated extended intercourse between the population of the towns& cities with the country. The cause of Hon Carlos (according to our correspondent) was about to merge into a more general one. which would set aside his pretensions to the throne.

The Madrid journals and correspondence of the loth and 17th have reached us. The communications between the government and General Espartero had been of late exceedingly active. The government hoped to avail itself of the good dispositions of General .Marotto and of the people of the northern provinces to bring the civil war to a speedy and satisfactory termination. Gen- Marotto had lately written a most affectionate letter to Gen. Espartero, recommending to him a Carlist colonel, who had fallen into the hands of the Christinos. The reply of the Queen's general to this letter was an order to set the prisoner at liberty.

Advices from Bayonne of the 21st instant state, that there was nothing new at Tolusa on the 18th, nor along the line of Andosin þÿ Tne country enjoyed a most perfect tranquility. Marotto's head quarters were siiil at Estella, where he was busily engaged in organising the army. He had already formed four Castiliinu battalions 900 men strong. þÿ The Archbishop of Cuba (Father Cyril), who had recovered from a severe indisposition, transacted business directly with Don Carlos. The President of the Council had not yet been appointed þÿ St. Thomas Times May 1.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, Apnl 23, 1833. QUEEN VICTORIA. The Richmond Enquirer publishes a letter from Mr Stevenson, our Minister to Great Britain, in which he describes the person, ap- P .uauce, and habits of the Queen of Great Britain Mr. Stevenson writes from opportu ities of close and frequent observation, which few persons, even of the highest rank in the kingdom, can have had. He says : þÿ termined to have the best boats ( )f the Queen, I suppose you will expect me to say something, and express my opinion. þÿ The press in both countries gives the most fl titering accounts of her beauty, wisdom, &c. Indeed, it is the fashion here to represent her (as 1 suppose they do all Queens) as something short only of Divinity. Now, l will tell you verv frankly what I think ol her, and 1 have had a fair opportunity of judging. As to her person and face, they are pretty fairly represented in many of the numerous paintings and prints, some of which I suppose you have seen. þÿSully I s think as good and pleasing c a likeness as anv " that has been taken. It has been sent to Philadelphia. None ol them, however, do justice to the expression of the face It is certainly not the sort I should call beautiful, þÿ but, when lighted up by animated conversation, the face is full of expression and sweetness, and strongly indicative of character. Her manners are bland and unaffected ; indeed, there is a simplicity and frankness and engaging affability about her quite remarkable for a Queen. Another Striking thing is, the total absence of all am-

bitious display or desire for admiration, which might be expected from so young person, a and she a Sovereign. No one can approach the present. Queen without being struck, not only with her easy and charming deportment, and that peculiar softness of disposition and temper, for which she is so remarkable, but with the entire seit command and repose of manner, which might be expected to guard a Sovereign of more advanced years and experience. She has, besides, all the characteristic bon nalurel and good temper of the English. In relation to the Queen's personal habits, I understand she rises between 8 and 9, breakfast at 10, devotes herself to business till 2, then exercises, generally on horseback, and that at a rapid pace, going at the rate of 10 or 12 miles an hour. Of her horsemanship 1 had an opportunity of judging, having myself been present in one of her excursions of 20 miles in about 2 hours : and 1 can assure you, if she does not ride like Causer, or hunt like Diana, she is vet one of the boldest and finest female riders I ever saw. Her attention to business is such, that I understand, if a despatch comes while she is at dinner, she commonly rises and attends to it. She has a turn and capacity for business, and will, as she advances, doubtless take even a deeper interest in affairs of stale than she does at present.
